  • The biggest adoption killer is a bad first experience with the wrong tool.
  • When output is weak, adjust the tool, the context and the prompt before you quit.
  • Treat AI like a team: generalists and specialists working together.

A scientist said that to me. Almost word for word. 'I don't use AI. I tried it for scientific papers, and it gave me papers that weren't even real.'

And you know what? He was right. That really happened to him. His conclusion, though? That AI isn't valuable. That part was wrong.

Because here's the thing. He didn't have a bad experience with AI. He had a bad experience with the wrong AI, asked to do the wrong job.

And that one mistake, repeated by millions of people, is the biggest reason people walk away from technology that could change their lives.

Today, we fix that.

0:50Welcome: Chase the Benefit, Not the Definition

Visual: Host on camera. Lower third: 'Dr. Malik Hakim | Author, Transformation with AI'. Slide: 'Chapter 1: AI in Simple Terms'.

Welcome to SolutionAgents, Transformation with AI. I'm Dr. Malik Hakim, and today we're going to go over Chapter 1: AI in Simple Terms.

This is part one of a three-part seminar. And I want to start by giving you permission to do something. Stop chasing the perfect definition of AI.

In this world there are thousands of terms. Buzzwords. Acronyms. Concepts that people throw around to sound smart. AI is one of them. And yes, AI matters. It matters a lot. But not because it's impressive. Not because it's a trend. Not because it's going to dominate headlines.

AI matters for one reason: because it can transform your life and your career. That's our focus.

On screenSlide, 'AI matters because it can transform your life and your career.'

So I'm going to speak about AI in very high-level terms. I'm not going to take you into the weeds. If you want model architectures, datasets, optimization strategies, that's a different book. This one isn't written for AI engineers.

This is written for people with real lives. People with jobs. People with families. People with bills. People with responsibilities. People with dreams that got put on hold.

Across this seminar, we'll cover four things. One: the different forms of AI. Two: how that matters to you, so you choose the right AI and don't waste your time. Three: why privacy is important, and not just for your documents. And four: demanding more from AI, what it has to be to truly transform your life.

On screenFour-part roadmap graphic. Parts 1 and 2 of the chapter highlighted for today.

Today, in Part 1, we take the first two. Part 2 is privacy. Part 3 is demanding more. Let's begin.

2:46The AI Family: LLMs, Machine Learning, Deep Learning

Visual: Diagram: 'The AI Family' (LLMs, ML, Deep Learning and specialist models, LAMs).

On screenDiagram, 'AI is a family of tools.' Four tiles appear one at a time.

When people say 'AI,' they talk as if it's one thing. A single machine. A single brain. A single product. But AI is not one thing. AI is a family of tools. Different models, different ways of thinking, different strengths, different limitations.

And if you understand that at a basic level, you'll stop making the most common mistake: using the wrong AI for the wrong purpose, and then concluding AI isn't useful.

Let's meet the family. First, the one you've probably met: the large language model, or LLM.

These are the systems you talk to. You type something in, and it answers in text that sounds human. They're trained on enormous amounts of language, books, websites, documents, so they learn the patterns in how language works.

In very simple terms, an LLM learns sequentially. After an 'A' certain letters can follow. After 'AN' certain letters can follow. It learns how words form. Then sentences. Then paragraphs. Then whole structures.

Now here's something important. Many LLMs work like a black box. They can produce convincing language without always understanding the underlying reality the way a human expert would. That's why you hear about hallucinations: an answer that sounds right, delivered with confidence, and isn't real.

The good news is they're improving fast. Newer multimodal models have better contextual understanding. But the key point is simple. LLMs are often generalists. They can do many things. They may not be a specialist in the exact domain you need.

Ask one to help write an email, plan a trip, or explain a concept, and it can do that well. Ask it for highly specialized answers, without the right context or the right specialized system, and you may get weak output.

Next in the family: machine learning, or ML. ML often uses large datasets too, but it's usually built for a narrower scope. Classification. Prediction. Optimization. Detection. Pattern recognition.

When I described this originally, I used an onion-peel picture. You start at a high level, then peel toward deeper nuance, then narrow into a specific output. ML systems are extremely powerful at things like classifying images, predicting outcomes, spotting anomalies, optimizing a process. But most are not designed to answer every kind of question. They're built for a purpose, like a specialist in a profession.

On screenOnion-peel animation: broad ring, narrower ring, bullseye 'specific answer'.

Then there's deep learning and specialized models. These power speech recognition, image recognition, medical imaging analysis, recommendation systems. And there are specialized AIs for image processing, video, voice generation and transcription, coding, data analytics, and workflow automation. Within their narrow lane, these can be best in class.

5:54AI That Takes Action: Large Action Models

Visual: Split screen: 'Assistant that talks' vs 'Assistant that does'. Checklist animation.

Now to one of the most important developments, especially for everyday life and business: what I call large action models, or LAMs.

These are AIs that don't just generate text. They take action. They can send emails. Schedule meetings. Create calendar invites. Trigger workflows. Execute commands.

In other words, they move from an assistant that talks to an assistant that does. And that matters, because when AI can act, it stops being a novelty and becomes infrastructure.

On screenSplit screen. Left: 'Talks' with a drafted email. Right: 'Does' with email sent, meeting booked, task created.

Let me show you what that looks like. Meet Tanya. She's an operations lead, and she's drowning in micro-admin. Not big projects. The little things that silently destroy performance. Follow-up emails. Scheduling. Reminders. Action items. 'Did we ever send that?' 'Who owns this?' 'What did we decide?'

She tried a general AI for writing emails. Helpful, sure. But it didn't move the work forward. It didn't schedule the meeting. It didn't send the email. It didn't set the reminder.

Then she moved to an AI workflow with action capability. Now the AI didn't just draft the message. It created the email and scheduled the follow-up. It generated the meeting agenda and created the calendar invites. It summarized decisions and turned them into tasks.

Her day didn't just get faster. It got cleaner. She stopped carrying everything in her head.

And this isn't only for offices. Take Marco, a validation lead in a regulated manufacturing environment. His real job isn't only engineering. It's controlled templates, approved wording, revision history, document routing, audit-ready traceability.

A general AI helped him with wording, but it didn't build the task list, track approvals, or remind stakeholders. When he moved to AI that supports actions, it drafted the protocol skeleton in the right template structure, generated the validation checklist and assigned owners, created the meeting agenda and tracker, and drafted the follow-up emails from that tracker.

Marco still owned the final version. Accountability in a regulated setting is real. But the admin burden collapsed.

The lesson: if your problem is execution, you don't only need AI that writes. You need AI that can act.

8:25Generalists vs. Specialists, and the Three Components of Any AI

Visual: Diagram: 'Three components of every AI': Way of thinking, Knowledge base, Experience.

A simple way to hold all of this in your head is to compare AI to people.

Some people are generalists. I'm a generalist as a human being. I know a lot about a lot of things, and that's how I built my career. I also knew I never wanted to be a specialist in just one area, because that would mean dedicating my whole life to one narrow lane.

Machine learning models often resemble specialists, amazing at one job. LLMs often resemble generalists, good at many tasks. Neither is better. The only question is: which one do you need right now?

On screenTwo portraits: 'The Generalist' and 'The Specialist'. Caption: 'Which one do you need right now?'

Now, from a high level, every AI system has three components that shape what it can do for you.

One: a way of thinking. That's the personality of the model. The worldview, the style, the mathematical structure behind how it reasons. Ask two models the same question and you may get two different answers. Both can be correct, just from a different perspective.

Two: a knowledge base. What was it trained on? What can it access? What was included, and what was left out? Different knowledge base, different strengths.

Three: experience. The system learns from usage patterns, interaction history, and the way people work with it. That's why some people get emotionally attached to older models. They liked the personality, the behavior, the feel. Even if newer models know more, the older one sometimes feels better.

On screenThree-circle diagram builds, then lands on the line 'You're not choosing a brand. You're choosing a way of thinking, a knowledge base, and an experience.'

That's it. If you understand those basic differences, you're already ahead of most people, because you'll stop treating AI like one thing, and start treating it like a toolbox.

10:24The Bad-First-Experience Trap

Visual: Story segment. Illustrated timeline of Omar/Leena's experience. Checklist of 'verify' failures appears.

Now let's answer the real question. How does all of this matter to you?

It matters because the difference between AI being life-changing and AI being useless often comes down to one thing. Did you use the right AI for the right purpose?

When we ran analysis through Higgins to understand why people adopt AI or reject it, one of the most surprising insights was this: a lot of people avoid AI simply because of a bad first experience. They tried a tool. It gave a shallow answer. It hallucinated. It produced garbage. And they concluded, 'AI isn't valuable.'

Let me make that concrete. Let's call him Omar. He's a bench scientist. Everyone around him is talking about AI, so he tries it for a literature review. He asks a general chatbot for citations.

The output looks impressive. Authors, journals, years, even identifiers. But when he tries to locate the papers, several don't exist. Titles are wrong. Authors are wrong. Journals are wrong. He gets burned.

On screenChecklist with red marks: 'Paper doesn't exist', 'Invalid identifier', 'Wrong authors', 'Journal issue doesn't match year'.

His conclusion is immediate: 'AI is unreliable. I'm not using it.' In a scientific setting, credibility is everything, so you can understand the reaction.

But the problem wasn't AI. The problem was the type of AI, and the expectation. He used a generalist language model and asked it to behave like a scientific research librarian. Wrong form of AI for the job.

So Omar tries again, and this time he changes the request. Instead of asking for final answers, he asks: 'Give me ten keywords and Boolean search strings.' 'List the databases and how to search them.' 'Show me how to verify each citation.' 'Only include sources you can link to, and label anything uncertain.' He even asks it to build a literature matrix: claim, evidence, limitations, relevance.

Now AI is what it should have been all along. A powerful guide. Not a hallucination machine. It's a fast research assistant that structures his workflow without pretending to be the source of truth.

I give professionals a simple challenge. You know I'm a generalist. Would you trust me to pick the best insurance policy for your client? The best home? Develop the best chemistry for your product? Design the best instrument for your invention?

Every one of them says, 'Absolutely not. You're not qualified.' Exactly. So why would you take a generalist AI, trained broadly, and expect it to behave like a specialist in your profession, your regulatory environment, your business context?

If you want to bake bread, almost any general LLM can help. If you want to develop new chemistry for an implantable eye product, you need a different class of AI: specialized, contextual, supported by domain knowledge and verification.

On screenThree diagnostic questions, one at a time.

So here's the practical rule. If AI disappointed you once, don't walk away. Diagnose. Ask: Was I using a generalist when I needed a specialist? Did the system have the right context? Did it have the right knowledge base and performance level?

Most people don't need less AI. They need the right AI.

14:03Mixed Intelligence: When One Model Isn't Enough

Visual: Child-sleep graphic with four inputs flowing into one plan. Then the executive board report story with before/after document layout.

Some problems are multifaceted. They need both specialized knowledge and broad lived experience.

Say you want the best sleep pattern for your child. You want specialized child development knowledge. You want experience patterns from other parents. You want practical 'what actually worked' insights. And you want guidance that respects your family's context.

No single model is the best at all four. That's where multiple AIs working together become powerful, specialists plus generalists. It's part of what we built into Higgins: the concept of multiple AI teams working together, instead of one model doing everything. Because real life is not one-dimensional.

On screenFour inputs, 'Specialist knowledge', 'Parent experience', 'What worked', 'Your family context', flow into 'One plan'.

Let me give you one more example of the right AI changing an outcome. An executive had to write a performance review for her board. That's hard, because self-evaluations are naturally subjective. You highlight your wins, and the board knows it. It can feel self-serving, even when you're doing great.

She also had a separate document: a 360 evaluation from her leadership team. Strengths, weaknesses, development areas. She asked, 'How do I combine these into something objective?'

She put both into Higgins, where the AI was already trained on her company context, her objectives, her language style, her internal structure. And Higgins produced an objective, KPI-style report: strengths and accomplishments, weaknesses and development needs, a balanced summary, all in a board-ready tone.

She sent it to the board, noting it was supported by Higgins AI to ensure objectivity.

That's powerful for two reasons. First, it improves quality beyond what you can do alone, because you can't fully be objective about yourself. Second, it creates credibility, structure and professionalism that can change how people perceive your leadership.

That's transformation. Not in theory. In the real world.

Key takeaways

  • Privacy includes documents and interactions: prompts, workflows, decision criteria and operational logic.
  • Free, paid and enterprise AI differ. Even paid tools may still learn from you, so validate the policy.
  • Trade secrets can leak through how you work, even when no document is shared.
  • In regulated work, treat AI like any other system: validate, protect controlled content, get permission.
  • Use the boundary box: get permission, sanitize inputs, protect confidentials.

  4. Where should the line be for AI use at work: policy, permission, de-identification, approved tools?

0:00Cold Open

Visual: Starfield. A glowing document icon with a lock fades in, then a second, fainter layer labeled 'how you work' appears behind it.

On screenQuestion types in: 'What if your most valuable secret was never in a document?'

Picture an injury law firm with a remarkably successful intake process. A caller phones in, and within minutes the firm knows whether this is a case worth taking. That screening method is a big part of why the firm is profitable.

It isn't patented. It isn't written up as a formula. It's a learned method, refined over years.

Now imagine the firm starts using AI to speed up intake. They never upload a document. Not one. And yet, over time, the thing that makes them special may quietly walk out the door.

How? That's today's episode.

On screenLogo sting. Title card: 'Part 2: Privacy Is Your Competitive Advantage'.

0:46Privacy Is Foundational

Visual: Host on camera. Slide: 'Privacy is not a side feature.'

Welcome back to SolutionAgents, Transformation with AI. I'm Dr. Malik Hakim, and this is Part 2: Why Privacy Is Important.

In Part 1 we learned that AI is a family of tools, and that choosing the right one matters. Now we need to talk about something I want to be very clear on.

Privacy is not a side feature. Privacy is not a nice-to-have. Privacy is foundational.

On screenSlide, three short lines: 'Not a side feature. Not a nice-to-have. Foundational.'

Why? Because if AI is going to transform your life, you have to trust it. And trust comes from privacy.

1:26Privacy Is More Than Documents

Visual: Diagram: concentric layers of privacy. Center: Documents. Outward: Prompts, Workflows, Decision criteria, Operational logic.

Most people hear 'privacy' and think: are my documents safe? That's part of it. But AI adds a second layer.

AI doesn't just store information. AI learns from information. And AI doesn't only learn from documents. It learns from your interactions.

On screenConcentric-rings diagram builds from the center outward.

So privacy is about what you upload. What you say. How you work. How you make decisions. What patterns you reveal. What processes your business runs on.

Think about the layers. At the center, your documents. Around them, your prompts, the questions you ask. Around that, your workflows, the order in which you do things. Around that, your decision criteria, how you decide yes or no. And on the outside, your operational logic, your 'how we do it.'

That's why privacy matters even if you never upload a single PDF.

2:25Free, Paid and Enterprise AI

Visual: Three-column comparison: Free, Paid, Enterprise. Bottom banner: 'Validate the policy.'

So how do the different kinds of tools compare? In general terms, free AI tools often provide the lowest level of privacy. Paid tools often provide more privacy, but not always full privacy. Enterprise tools can be designed for higher privacy, but you have to validate the policies.

On screenThree columns with a gradient from 'lowest' to 'designed for higher'. Footnote: 'General terms. Always verify the provider's policy.'

And here's the key point. Even paid systems may still learn from you. They may not publish your document. But the learning from your interactions can become part of broader model improvement.

So 'I pay for it' is not the same sentence as 'it's private.' Read the policy. Ask the question directly: does this system learn from my conversations, and what happens to what it learns?

3:16The Law Firm Story: Trade Secrets Through Interaction

Visual: Animated flow: Firm A's intake questions flow into the AI; the AI's improved screening logic flows out to Firm B.

Let's go back to our injury law firm. Remember, they have a successful intake process, a method of screening callers to decide whether there's a case worth pursuing. It's not patented. It's, in many ways, a trade secret.

They want AI to speed things up, so they start typing prompts like: 'Here's how we screen callers.' 'Here are our decision rules.' 'Here's how we decide yes or no.' They feel safe, because they're not uploading documents.

On screenThree prompts appear in a chat bubble, labeled 'No documents uploaded'.

But the risk isn't only the documents. The risk is the interaction. The decision criteria. The workflow logic. The screening questions. The trade-secret process itself.

Even if the system doesn't publish their text, the AI may learn from how they screen, what questions they ask, what criteria they use, how they decide, how they structure those decisions.

If the AI uses those learnings in aggregate, another firm can ask: 'What's the best way to screen applicants for an injury firm?' And the AI produces a stronger screening model, built partly from that first firm's private process, and partly from others.

Does that reduce the first firm's competitive edge? Yes.

On screenFlow animation completes. Caption: 'Privacy is not only about keeping documents hidden. It's about protecting the way you operate.'

That's the lesson. Privacy is not only about keeping documents hidden. It's about protecting the way you operate.

4:48The Biotech Story: Documents AND Interactions

Visual: Illustrated scenario of a CMC team. Callouts: 'mixing order', 'temperature windows', 'hold times', 'in-process controls'.

Now let's move to a regulated world. Biotech and pharma, where privacy is not only a competitive issue but a compliance one.

Imagine a CMC group at a growing biotech. They have a process advantage for scaling a sensitive formulation. How they adjust mixing order. Temperature windows. Hold times. In-process controls that keep quality attributes stable during scale-up.

Most of this isn't written down as a trade secret. It lives in internal decision logic, recurring meetings, troubleshooting playbooks, and the tacit know-how of a few key people.

A team member starts using a public AI tool to help write documents. 'Here's how we decide whether a batch is at risk.' 'Here's our troubleshooting logic.' 'Here's the decision tree we use when viscosity drifts.'

They think they're safe, because they never uploaded a full controlled document. But the risk was never only the files. The risk was the interaction. The process logic itself.

On screenText: 'Even if the AI never publishes your SOP, it can learn patterns from your decision workflow and generalize them.'

Over time, another company or consultant could ask, 'What's the best troubleshooting decision tree for viscosity drift during scale-up?' And the answer could reflect learned patterns from many users, possibly including that CMC team's unique method.

In life sciences, this is more than embarrassment. It can dilute competitive advantage, create IP exposure, and raise compliance concerns if confidential content is mishandled.

If you work in a GxP environment, here's the line to remember: treat AI like any other system. Validate the workflow. Protect controlled content. And never upload regulated or proprietary material without approved tools and permission.

The high-risk zones are easy to name. Regulated documents: SOPs, batch records, deviations, CAPAs, change controls. And trade secrets: screening criteria, intake scripts, pricing logic, internal methods.

6:49Change Control: The Small Change That Wasn't Small

Visual: Before/after of a change-control draft. Checklist of impact domains: equipment, process parameters, training, documentation, validation, supply chain.

Let me show you what good privacy discipline looks like in a regulated setting. Meet Sam, a process engineer. He needs to make what looks like a minor change: adjust a mixing speed range and update a work instruction to reduce variability.

In normal life, that's a simple edit. In a GMP environment, it becomes a change control.

Sam opens a general AI tool and says, 'Write a change control justification.' The result is polished, but generic. No clear scope boundaries. No structured impact assessment across equipment qualification, cleaning validation, labeling, training, downstream steps. No link to validation expectations. No risk-based rationale consistent with internal quality standards.

The danger is subtle. A generic change control can pass internal review once, and then become painful later at inspection, when someone asks, 'Show me how you assessed impact, and why you concluded no re-validation was required.'

On screenChecklist builds: Equipment, Process parameters, Training, Documentation, Validation, Supply chain.

So Sam redoes it the right way. He uses his company's change control template and required headings. He has the AI generate an impact assessment checklist across those domains. He demands a risk-based framing and a list of the evidence he'd need. And he asks for a clean implementation plan: owners, dates, dependencies, a back-out plan.

And critically, he protects privacy. He doesn't paste proprietary formulas or vendor contracts into a random tool. He keeps inputs sanitized, or uses an approved private environment.

The result reads like it was written by a cross-functional team, because the AI helped him think across domains. Fewer review cycles. Fewer 'please add' comments from QA. Fewer surprises.

The goal isn't faster paperwork. It's fewer regulatory surprises and better decision quality, with privacy intact.

8:48Permission, Policy and the Personalization Trade-off

Visual: Host on camera. Slide: 'Privacy is not paranoia. Privacy is professionalism.' Two-column graphic: 'Personal' pulls toward sharing, 'Private' pulls toward protecting.

Before we get practical, two ideas that trip people up.

The first is permission. If you work in a company that has private documents, you must have permission before uploading anything into any AI tool. Not forgiveness afterward. Permission before. If you own a business with unique processes, you must protect your methods and your strategy.

On screenSlide: 'Permission first.' Beneath it: 'Ask: Is this tool approved? Who owns this material? What does the policy say?'

Three questions will keep you out of trouble. Is this tool approved for this kind of material? Who owns the material I'm about to share? And what does the provider's policy say happens to my inputs?

The second idea is a tension I want you to be honest about. The more personal an AI becomes, the more it needs to learn about you. And the more it learns about you, the more privacy matters. Personal pulls you toward sharing. Private pulls you toward protecting.

On screenTwo arrows pulling in opposite directions, meeting at a lock.

You don't resolve that tension by avoiding personalization. You resolve it by choosing a system where the learning stays yours, and by deciding in advance what you will never share. We'll come back to this in Part 3, because it's exactly why a safe space is a prerequisite for growth.

For now, hold on to this: privacy is not paranoia. Privacy is professionalism.

10:20The Work vs. Personal Boundary Box

Visual: Graphic: Boundary Box with three scenarios, each with DO and DON'T columns.

Now let's make this practical. I want you to use a simple tool I call the Work versus Personal boundary box. Three examples.

On screenBoundary Box graphic. Example 1 highlighted.

Example one. Work, and safe. You need to write a weekly project update to leadership. Do: paste a sanitized outline. 'Project X status: on track. Risk: vendor delay. Ask: approve budget change.' Then ask the AI to turn it into a one-page executive update with bullets, risks, mitigations and next steps. Don't: paste internal financials, customer names, contract terms, unreleased roadmap details, or screenshots of internal systems. You get clarity and speed without leaking strategy.

Example two. Work, and not safe, unless you do it right. You want help rewriting an SOP, an operations manual, or an internal playbook. Do: get permission, and use an approved private or enterprise AI, or a controlled environment. Give structure without secrets: 'Here are the section headers we require. Draft a generic SOP template for this process.' Don't: upload the full manual into a random free tool, or describe your company's unique decision criteria, your secret sauce, in chat. Even if the document isn't published, the process logic can be learned from.

Example three. Personal, safe and powerful. You want a weekly routine for your household: meals, chores, school logistics. Do: use placeholders. 'Child A, age eight. Child B, age twelve.' Share preferences without identifiers: allergies, time constraints, budget range, schedule blocks. Then ask for a weekly meal plan, a grocery list and a Sunday reset checklist. Don't: paste your children's full names, school, home address, medical record numbers or account logins. You get lower mental load and better planning without exposing the most sensitive identifiers.

On screenThree rules in large type: 'Get permission. Sanitize inputs. Protect confidentials.'

Three rules to take away. Always get permission before using AI on workplace materials. Redact personal and health information. And protect company confidentials.

12:33Our Privacy Philosophy, Factually

Visual: Host on camera. Slide with four short statements. Footer: 'Always verify privacy policies, wherever you go.'

I'd like to share how we think about this at Higgins, and I'll keep it factual. Higgins was built with privacy as a core pillar. We do not sell chats. We do not sell conversation learnings. We do not sell documents. Privacy is part of the design, not an add-on.

On screenFour statements, one at a time.

And to be fair, Higgins is not the only company that takes privacy seriously. But you must verify privacy policies wherever you go. Because the moment AI becomes personal, the moment it becomes a guide, the moment it becomes part of your daily pattern, privacy becomes non-negotiable.

And one more thing. Privacy is not paranoia. Privacy is professionalism.

0:00Cold Open

Visual: Starfield. Robot-looking-up image. Text types in: 'AI is not here just to write better emails.'

On screen'AI is not here just to write better emails.' Then: 'Or summarize documents.' Then: 'Or plan a trip.'

AI is not here just to write better emails. AI is not here just to summarize documents. AI is not here just to plan a trip.

That's fine. That's fun. That's baby level. But that's not the true power of AI.

Today we raise the bar.

On screenLogo sting. Title card: 'Part 3: Demand More From AI'.

0:25Why Baby Steps Aren't Enough

Visual: Host on camera. Slide: 'Demand that it transforms the way you live and the way you work.'

Welcome back to SolutionAgents, Transformation with AI. I'm Dr. Malik Hakim, and this is the final part of our Chapter 1 seminar: Demanding More From AI.

In Part 1 you learned that AI is a family of tools and that the right AI matters. In Part 2 you learned that privacy covers your documents and your interactions.

Now I want you to hear me clearly. We need to demand more. I'm asking you, as the viewer, the listener, the reader, to demand more from AI. Demand that it transforms the way you live and the way you work.

And for AI to truly do that, I believe it must meet three requirements. It must be personal. It must be private. And it must perform.

On screenThree-requirements diagram: three overlapping circles labeled Personal, Private, Performs. Center: 'Transformation'.

1:20Requirement 1: AI Must Be Personal

Visual: List builds: how you write, how you think, what you like, what you don't, your standards, goals, constraints.

Requirement one: AI must be personal. Your AI must understand you.

It has to learn how you write. How you think. What you like. What you don't like. What your standards are. What your goals are. What your constraints are. And that understanding has to grow over time.

On screenSeven items appear one at a time, then fade into a single 'You' silhouette.

This is relationship-building. Just like any relationship with a person, trust and performance improve as you work together.

And here's the part people don't expect. When AI becomes personal, it becomes more invisible. The output becomes so relevant and so intuitive that you don't have to fight it. Eventually, using your AI becomes natural. You don't even think about 'using AI.' It's part of how you think and work.

That's when transformation begins.

2:15Requirement 2: AI Must Be Private

Visual: Graphic: a locked room labeled 'Safe space'. Items inside: stupid questions, ideas, uncertainty, plans, roadmaps, iterations.

Requirement two: AI must be private. Personal without privacy is not support. It's risk.

If your conversations can be learned from and sold, or if your processes can be absorbed into broader public knowledge, you cannot trust the system fully. And without trust, you won't transform. Because transformation requires experimentation.

On screenLocked room graphic. Items fade in.

You need a safe space to ask the stupid questions. To explore ideas. To admit uncertainty. To build plans. To test roadmaps. To iterate without being exposed.

A private environment is a prerequisite for real growth. If you only ask the AI the questions you're comfortable having on a billboard, you're only getting a fraction of the benefit.

3:04Requirement 3: AI Must Perform

Visual: Checklist of failure modes: hallucinates, shallow, too much, too little, can't operate in your domain.

Requirement three, and this one is critical: AI must perform. At the level you need, consistently.

Because if your AI hallucinates, if it gives shallow answers, if it gives you too much when you need less, if it gives you too little when you need more, if it can't operate in your domain, then AI becomes a burden, not a gift.

On screenChecklist items cross out one at a time.

And then what happens? You conclude, 'AI isn't valuable.' We're right back where we started in Part 1.

That's why performance isn't a detail. It's the foundation. The right AI must fit like a glove. Personal. Private. High-performing.

On screenGlove graphic. Three words light up.

When those three are present, AI stops being a novelty and becomes a life partner.

3:57Three People, Three Requirements

Visual: Three-card layout: Omar (Performs), the executive (Personal), the law firm (Private). Each card shows 'What was missing' and 'What changed'.

Let me connect these three requirements to people you've already met in this seminar, because I think this is where it clicks.

On screenThree cards slide in side by side.

Remember Omar, the scientist who got fake citations? What was missing for him was performance. The AI couldn't operate in his domain, and it wasn't asked to show its work. When he demanded search strings, verification steps and labeled uncertainty, performance became something he could check, and his relationship with AI changed.

Remember the executive writing her board report? What made it work was that the AI was already personal. It knew her company context, her objectives, her language style, her internal structure. That's why the output came back in a board-ready tone instead of generic filler. She didn't have to fight it.

And remember the injury law firm? What was missing was privacy. They had personal and they had performance, but they were feeding their screening logic into a system that could generalize it. A great tool, in an unsafe room.

Notice the pattern. Take away any one of the three and the value collapses. Personal and private, but it hallucinates: you can't rely on it. Private and performs, but generic: it never fits your life. Personal and performs, but not private: it's a risk to everything that makes you valuable.

On screenThree-circle diagram, with each missing-circle case highlighted in turn.

That's why I say the right AI fits like a glove. Not because it's flashy. Because all three are present at once, and you stop thinking about the tool and start thinking about the work.

5:49How to Demand More: Eight Prompts and a Template

Visual: Eight prompt cards, then the five-line Demand-More template (Goal, Context, Output format, Quality bar, Privacy rule).

So how do you actually demand more? No technical background required. Here are simple prompts you can use today.

On screenPrompt cards appear one at a time.

One: 'Ask me the questions you need before answering.' Two: 'Give me three options, then recommend one.' Three: 'Explain your reasoning step by step.' Four: 'List assumptions and what information you're missing.' Five: 'Translate this into a plan I can execute in thirty minutes a day.' Six: 'Format this to match my organization's style.' Seven: 'Help me build a roadmap: next three steps, not the next three hundred.' And eight, my favorite: 'Challenge me. What am I not seeing?'

This is how AI becomes more than a tool. This is how it becomes your assistant, your strategist, your guide.

Now let me give you a template. We use this in our book club. Five lines.

Goal: what you're trying to do. Context: who is involved, and what the constraints are. Output format: bullets, a table, steps, a template. Quality bar: 'cite sources,' 'use our template,' 'ask questions first.' And privacy rule: 'no names,' 'sanitize,' 'don't store.'

On screenThe five-line template, with a worked example filled in: 'Goal: a 7-day plan to cut one admin burden. Context: two kids, two jobs, 30 minutes a day. Output: table by day. Quality bar: ask me questions first. Privacy rule: no names.'

Try it right now on one real task. It takes five minutes, and it will change the answer you get.

7:18Case Study: The Deviation That Could Have Become an Audit Finding

Visual: Story segment. Left column: 'Generic AI draft' with gaps. Right column: 'Demanded structure' with Event Summary through Effectiveness Check.

Let me show you what demanding more looks like in the hardest of settings: a regulated environment.

Meet Nina, a QA specialist supporting manufacturing in a GMP facility. An operator recorded a hold time outside the validated window. The immediate issue is clear. The pressure is what comes next. The deviation write-up will be read by quality leadership, possibly regulators, and definitely auditors.

She asks a general AI tool to help draft the narrative. It produces a confident-looking report that misses the regulated logic. A weak distinction between immediate correction, corrective action and preventive action. Root cause reasoning that jumps to conclusions. No structured statement of product impact. No CAPA traceability: who owns what, by when, and how effectiveness is measured.

On screenLeft column with four red gaps.

It sounds good. It wouldn't survive an audit. So Nina demands more, and she uses AI as a co-writer with a regulated structure.

She asks: 'Draft the deviation in this exact structure: Event Summary, Impact Assessment, Investigation, Root Cause, CAPA, Effectiveness Check.' 'List the assumptions and missing facts I must confirm.' 'Give me three root cause hypotheses, with the evidence needed for each.' 'Propose CAPAs that are measurable, time-bound, and linked to the root cause.' And: 'Create an effectiveness check plan: what metric, what timeframe, what pass-fail criteria.'

On screenRight column builds, step by step.

Then she applies what I call the 90:10 mindset. The AI drafts the structure, the wording and the CAPA options, that's the ninety. Nina verifies the facts, aligns with site procedures, checks the compliance language and ensures traceability, that's the ten. And that ten is the expert part: truth, judgment, compliance.

Her package becomes clearer, more defensible and easier to review. Instead of fighting a blank page under pressure, she focuses on what only she can do.

In regulated environments, AI that writes well isn't enough. You need AI that can operate inside the logic of your field, and you must demand traceability, structure and verification.

9:38Your Three-Step Roadmap

Visual: Closing synthesis: three icons (Choose, Protect, Demand). Roadmap graphic: 'Next 3 steps, not the next 300.'

Let's pull the whole chapter together. You don't need to understand AI in the weeds. You need to understand how to get the benefit. And that comes down to three things.

On screenThree icons appear: Choose the right AI. Protect privacy. Demand personal, private and performance.

One: choose the right AI. Generalist or specialist, talker or doer, with the right context and the right expectations. Two: protect privacy. Documents, interactions, workflows, trade secrets. Permission first, sanitize inputs, protect confidentials. Three: demand personal, private and performance.

And when you're ready to act, keep it small. Next three steps, not the next three hundred.

Here are the practical actions I'd leave you with. Start with a low-risk use case to build confidence. Before you use AI at work, get permission, sanitize inputs and protect confidentials. Use AI for frameworks and drafts, then verify and finalize. When output is weak, don't quit. Adjust the tool, the context and the prompt. And demand the five behaviors: explain your reasoning, list assumptions and missing inputs, provide three options, format to my standard, and give me the next three steps.
